title: J.B. Hunt Shares Sink 13% After Warning Q3 Earnings Will Fall
excerpt: CFO Brad Delco said third-quarter earnings will fall 5% to 10% from the second quarter as $25 million in driver costs and surging diesel prices squeeze margins — a rare intra-quarter warning that sent the stock to its steepest drop of the year.
body:
• Chief Financial Officer Brad Delco told a Morgan Stanley investor conference Tuesday that J.B. Hunt expects third-quarter earnings to fall 5% to 10% sequentially — a rare intra-quarter warning from a company that ordinarily gives no guidance.
  • The implied third-quarter EPS of roughly $1.72 to $1.81 would land 15% to 20% below Wall Street's $2.09 estimate, which had anticipated 9% sequential earnings growth.
  • Delco cited about $25 million in incremental driver-related costs, at least a $10 million fuel headwind, and higher insurance claims, with diesel above $6 a gallon — up roughly 68% from a year ago.
  • Shares fell about 13% Wednesday to around $237, leading S&P 500 decliners, even as analysts said demand remains strong and the cost hit looks temporary.

J.B. Hunt Transport Services delivered an unusual warning on Tuesday: its third-quarter earnings will decline rather than grow. Chief Financial Officer Brad Delco, speaking at the Morgan Stanley Laguna Industrials Conference, said the freight shipper expects earnings to drop 5% to 10% from the second quarter — a rare move for a company that does not ordinarily provide explicit financial guidance.

The market's verdict was swift. Shares of J.B. Hunt (JBHT) fell nearly 13% in Wednesday trading, making it the leading decliner in the S&P 500, according to Barron's, and closed at $236.73, down $36.32 or 13.3%, Talk Business & Politics reported.

Context & Background

Wall Street had been expecting the opposite. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha projected third-quarter earnings would grow 9% sequentially, and consensus called for EPS of $2.09, up from $1.76 a year ago, according to Barron's. Delco's update implies EPS of roughly $1.72 to $1.81 — 15% to 20% below Street estimates, per Stephens Inc.

The culprit is costs arriving faster than pricing can adjust. Between recruiting, advertising, onboarding, training, sign-on bonuses and pay raises, the company expects about $25 million more in driver-related costs in the third quarter than in the second, Delco said. Fuel adds at least another $10 million sequential headwind, alongside higher claims costs as medical expenses outpace general inflation, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Diesel is the heaviest weight. It is north of $6 a gallon, up from about $3.70 a year ago and reaching $6.29 this week — up 68% year over year, per the Journal. Diesel has risen faster than gasoline or crude partly because the US-Iran war has sapped heavy crude from the market, the oil type best suited for making diesel.

"We have seen some of the most radical and abnormal swings in fuel prices that we've ever seen."

— Brad Delco, Chief Financial Officer, J.B. Hunt Transport Services

Driver hiring is the second pressure point. US businesses have reported a shortage of truck drivers as federal officials limit the number of immigrants eligible to drive commercial vehicles, the Journal reported. Delco framed the $25 million as growth spending — hiring ahead of demand — rather than pure inflation.

Impact & Analysis

The warning stings partly because the stock had been on a strong run: J.B. Hunt earned more than $9 a share in 2022 and about $6 a share in 2025, and Wall Street expects about $7.75 for 2026, according to FactSet data cited by Barron's.

Analysts argued the pain is likely timing rather than structural. StoneX analyst Christopher Kuhn wrote that demand remains strong, and that the spread between truckload and intermodal pricing has widened to "historically attractive levels" — favorable for J.B. Hunt's intermodal business, which benefits when high diesel prices push shippers toward rail.

"It really is more of a timing issue. I think you can look at a glass half-empty or a glass half-full. I'm really glad that we have visibility to these costs right now."

— Brad Delco, Chief Financial Officer, J.B. Hunt Transport Services

Stephens analysts agreed the headwinds look "temporary/timing in nature," pointing to a dedicated-segment backlog above peak Covid levels and intermodal pricing discussions for 2027 beginning in October — a chance for cost recovery and margin expansion. Still, Barron's noted that high diesel prices could also be denting shipping demand, a watch item for the entire freight sector.

Diaspora Angle

Freight sits one step behind the consumer economy in most portfolios, but the signal travels fast: rising diesel and driver costs eventually surface in goods prices and in the margins of retailers and manufacturers. Investors can treat the diesel-driven intermodal pricing advantage as a portfolio signal even without direct exposure to trucking.

What's Next

J.B. Hunt reports full third-quarter results in the coming weeks, and investors will look for confirmation that volumes are improving sequentially as Delco predicted. The October start of 2027 intermodal pricing discussions is the next test of whether the company can pass through higher costs.
